structure.title: Module 13: Conversation UI
structure.prefix_summary:
# Module 13: Conversation UI

Module 13 is the primary interface that sales reps interact with during every customer engagement. It is a real-time, state-driven application that reflects the current session’s context, active agent, discovery progress, and recommendations. Every visual element on screen is a function of the session state held in Module 1 (State Engine) and pushed to the UI via WebSocket.

nodes.title: 13.1 Layout Architecture
nodes.prefix_summary: This partial document section outlines the layout architecture of a Conversation UI designed for guided selling. It describes six main UI components—Chat Panel, Customer Context Panel, Discovery Progress, Recommendations Panel, Quick Actions Bar, and Agent Indicator—detailing their screen positions, purposes, and primary data sources. The layout is structured as a multi-panel workspace, enabling sales representatives to access all necessary information and tools within a single interface, eliminating the need to switch tabs or open separate applications. Each component is mapped to specific backend modules responsible for providing real-time data and context relevant to the sales conversation.

nodes.title: 13.1.1 Chat Panel — The Conversation Thread
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the Chat Panel component of a conversational interface between a representative and an AI assistant. It explains the visual layout (rep messages right-aligned in brand colors, AI messages left-aligned with a neutral background) and emphasizes that AI responses are structured, not free-form, and may include interactive elements like product links, discovery questions, and action suggestions. The Chat Panel is tightly integrated with the session state, updating in real time as new messages are added via a message rendering pipeline involving API calls, state management, and WebSocket events. The system aims for sub-2-second latency for message round-trips and provides a typing indicator for longer AI processing times.

nodes.title: 13.1.2 Customer Context Panel
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "Customer Context Panel" within a platform's user interface. It explains that the panel, located in the left sidebar, provides a read-only summary of all customer information available to the platform at the start and during a conversation. The panel is populated by integrating data from CRM and ERP systems via specific modules, and displays sections such as Account Header, Current Products, Key Metrics, Health Score, Recent Activity, and Relationship Map, each with their data sources and update frequencies. The document emphasizes that the panel is intentionally non-editable to prevent data conflicts, with any CRM data updates handled through a separate CRM Widget module, ensuring the Conversation UI remains focused on sales activities rather than data entry.

nodes.title: 13.1.3 Discovery Progress
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "Discovery Progress" component, which tracks and visualizes how much a sales representative has learned about a customer's needs across several predefined dimensions (such as Business Challenges, Current Infrastructure, Decision Timeline, and Budget Authority). It explains that in the MVP, these dimensions are fixed and equally weighted, with progress updated automatically based on conversation analysis. The UI displays this progress using simple progress bars. In the full product, dimensions and their weights are customizable per tenant via an admin portal, progress calculation is more nuanced (considering answer quality), and the visualization is enhanced with radar charts and color coding. The completion threshold for discovery is also configurable in the full product. The document includes a comparison table outlining these differences between the MVP and the full product.

nodes.title: 13.1.4 Recommendations Panel
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the Recommendations Panel, a UI component where intelligent product or solution suggestions are presented to sales representatives. It explains how recommendations are generated by agents, structured, and transmitted through the platform, detailing the information shown on each recommendation card (product name, confidence score, reasoning, supporting evidence, and action buttons). The document also covers the Accepted Products Tray, a sub-component that tracks products accepted by the rep during the session, influencing future recommendations and agent behavior. The Tray’s contents are stored in session state and accessed by agents to tailor subsequent suggestions.

nodes.title: 13.1.5 Quick Actions Bar
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the Quick Actions Bar, a dynamic UI component that displays interactive buttons based on the outputs of the Plugin SDK (M12). The bar updates in real-time according to the conversation state, showing or hiding buttons as plugin trigger conditions are met or unmet. When a user clicks a button, a request is sent to execute the corresponding plugin, which runs in a sandboxed environment, accesses platform APIs, and returns output rendered in the Side Panel without disrupting the main workflow. The document also details the various button states (active, disabled, hidden, loading, error), their visual treatments, and the conditions under which each state appears, ensuring clear user feedback and interaction.

nodes.title: 13.1.6 Agent Indicator
nodes.summary:
### 13.1.6 Agent Indicator

The Agent Indicator is a small but critical UI element that shows which workflow agent (M6–M11) is currently active. It displays as a badge in the top bar with the agent’s name and icon (e.g., “Cross-Sell” with a branching icon, “Renewal” with a refresh icon). When the Orchestrator in M2 detects that a different agent should take over (based on trigger conditions and conversation flow), the Agent Indicator shows a subtle animation and a “Suggested switch” tooltip. The rep can accept or dismiss the switch suggestion.

This element reinforces the “rep in control” principle: the platform never silently switches agents. The rep always sees what’s happening and can override. The agent transition is logged in M1’s state as an agent_transition event, which M16 (Feedback Engine) uses to track whether agent switches correlate with better outcomes.

nodes.title: 13.2 Real-Time Communication — WebSocket Protocol
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 13.2 Real-Time Communication — WebSocket Protocol

Module 13 is the only interface module that communicates primarily via WebSocket rather than REST API. This is a deliberate architectural choice: the Conversation UI needs sub-second updates for typing indicators, state changes, recommendation arrivals, and agent transitions. REST polling would introduce unacceptable latency and unnecessary load.

nodes.title: 13.2.1 Connection Lifecycle
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the connection lifecycle for a representative (rep) interacting with a platform via WebSocket. It outlines the sequential phases of the connection: initiating the connection with a WebSocket upgrade and JWT authentication, binding the session, subscribing to various state channels, enabling active bidirectional communication, maintaining the connection with periodic heartbeats, and handling disconnection events. Technical details include session management, message scoping, channel subscriptions, heartbeat intervals, and session persistence for resumability.

nodes.title: 13.2.2 Message Types — Server to Client
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines the different types of messages that a server can send to a client in a user interface context. For each message type, it specifies the payload structure and the corresponding UI action to be performed. The message types include state updates, chat message appends, surfacing recommendations, plugin triggers and results, agent transitions, typing indicators, discovery updates, and error notifications. The document details how each message affects the UI, such as updating panels, showing notifications, animating elements, and handling errors, with the goal of maintaining real-time, interactive, and responsive user experiences.

nodes.title: 13.2.3 Message Types — Client to Server
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines the main types of messages sent from client to server in a conversational application, detailing the payload structure and corresponding backend actions for each message type (such as sending messages, accepting or dismissing recommendations, executing plugins, switching agents, and sending feedback). It also explains the rationale for using WebSocket communication instead of REST, emphasizing the efficiency and real-time capabilities of WebSockets for handling frequent state updates in active sessions, reducing overhead and enabling instant server-to-client updates.

nodes.title: 13.3 State-Driven UI Rendering
nodes.summary: This partial document section explains the principle of state-driven UI rendering in Module 13, where all UI components are direct projections of the session state managed by M1. It emphasizes that the UI does not hold independent state; instead, it reconstructs entirely from persisted session state, ensuring no data loss on refresh. The document provides a table mapping each UI component to its corresponding state layer and the specific state fields it consumes. It describes the initial full state synchronization via API when the UI connects, followed by incremental state updates (deltas) over WebSocket to keep the UI responsive and bandwidth-efficient. The section also details the optimistic UI update pattern, where user actions (like sending a chat message) are rendered immediately and marked as pending until server confirmation. It explains how version numbers are used for conflict detection and resolution, triggering a full state re-sync if inconsistencies are detected.

nodes.title: 13.4 UX Principles — How They Translate to Code
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines how four key UX principles—Dynamic, Rep in Control, Progressive Disclosure, and Workflow Aware—are concretely implemented in code within a user interface. For each principle, the document explains its meaning and details the corresponding technical strategies: conditional rendering of UI elements based on state, ensuring user (rep) autonomy over AI suggestions, loading and displaying information contextually to minimize cognitive load, and adapting UI elements to reflect the active agent’s workflow. The section emphasizes the translation of abstract UX concepts into specific coding patterns and interface behaviors.

nodes.title: 13.5 Session Lifecycle from the UI Perspective
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines the session lifecycle from the perspective of the Conversation UI, detailing each phase a user (rep) experiences during a session. It describes the UI events and backend module interactions for each stage: starting a session, assembling customer context, initiating the conversation with an AI-generated greeting, conducting an active conversation with dynamic recommendations and agent transitions, surfacing product recommendations, enabling action-oriented Quick Actions (like generating emails or quotes), and finally ending the session with state persistence and audit logging. The document emphasizes the interplay between UI updates and backend processes, highlighting how context, agent selection, recommendations, and session data are managed throughout the session lifecycle.

nodes.title: 13.6 Module Access Map — What Module 13 Touches
nodes.summary:
This partial document outlines how Module 13 (M13) interacts with various backend modules in a system. It details the access methods, communication protocols, and data flow directions for each module. Key points include:

- M13 primarily uses WebSocket and REST to interact with the state engine (M1), enabling bidirectional communication for state reading and mutation.
- Access to other modules (M2 Orchestrator, M3 KB Engine, M4 Data Integration, M5 Multi-Tenancy) is mostly indirect, often mediated through M1 or backend agents/plugins, with data primarily read for context, configuration, and agent responses.
- Direct REST and WebSocket communication is used for plugin execution (M12 Plugin SDK), feedback signals (M16 Feedback Engine), and authentication (M18 Auth & Roles).
- Compliance (M19) is handled passively, with audits on state mutations via event subscriptions.
- All REST API calls are routed through the API Gateway (M20), which manages request routing and rate limiting.
- The document provides a clear mapping of how M13 accesses, communicates with, and exchanges data with each backend module, emphasizing the integration points and data flow directions.

structure.title: Module 14: CRM Embedded Widget
structure.prefix_summary:
# Module 14: CRM Embedded Widget

Module 14 takes the core capabilities of the Conversation UI and embeds them inside the rep’s CRM system — the application they already live in. The widget is not a miniaturized copy of Module 13; it is a purpose-built compact interface optimized for the CRM sidebar form factor. The goal: the rep should never need to leave their CRM to access platform intelligence.

nodes.title: 14.1 Supported CRM Platforms
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines the supported CRM platforms for a widget integration, specifically Salesforce and HubSpot. It details the integration types, rendering surfaces, and technical frameworks used for each platform: Salesforce utilizes Lightning Web Components (LWC) deployed as a managed package, while HubSpot uses a React-based iframe app registered via its App Marketplace. The document also explains the choice of REST API (with short polling) over WebSocket for communication, citing technical constraints such as strict Content Security Policies and cross-origin restrictions in CRM environments. It notes that Server-Sent Events (SSE) are considered for the full product as a compliant alternative for real-time updates.

nodes.title: 14.2 Auto-Context Detection
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 14.2 Auto-Context Detection

The most important capability of the CRM Widget is automatic context detection. When the rep navigates to a CRM record (Account, Opportunity, Contact), the widget automatically detects which record they’re viewing and loads the relevant session context — without the rep typing anything.

nodes.title: 14.2.1 Detection Mechanism per Platform
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes how a widget detects CRM context across different platforms (Salesforce LWC and HubSpot Sidebar). It outlines the detection mechanisms used on each platform to extract relevant CRM record data (such as Account ID, Opportunity ID, Object Type), and specifies fallback behaviors when context is unavailable (e.g., prompting manual account selection). The document also explains the process after context detection: the widget calls a Platform API to resolve the CRM record to an internal account, checks for active sessions, and either resumes or creates a session before rendering the session state.

nodes.title: 14.3 Widget Interface Components
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines the interface components of a CRM Widget, which is a streamlined version of components from Module 13, designed for use in a narrow sidebar. It presents a comparison table detailing how each major UI element from the full application is adapted for the widget. The main points covered include: the Mini Chat (a compact chat interface with limited formatting and features), Inline Recommendations (simplified, single-card recommendations with minimal evidence), Quick Action Chips (a scrollable row with a maximum of four visible actions), Context Summary (a collapsible header with key account information but without detailed maps or timelines), and Agent Badge (a simplified agent indicator without animations). The document emphasizes the reductions and changes made to each component to fit the widget’s space and usability constraints.

nodes.title: 14.4 CRM Write-Back
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the CRM Write-Back feature of a CRM Widget, highlighting its ability to log platform activities directly into CRM records for improved visibility among managers and team members. It details various write-back actions such as logging session activity, creating follow-up tasks, updating opportunity stages, attaching generated documents, and logging recommendation outcomes, specifying the type of CRM record updated, the data written, and the triggers for each action. The document also explains the write-back permission model, emphasizing the requirement for explicit OAuth scopes and adherence to CRM user permissions, ensuring that write-backs only occur when the user has appropriate access and providing error handling for insufficient permissions.

nodes.title: 14.5 Feature Parity Matrix — Module 13 vs Module 14
nodes.summary: This partial document presents a feature parity matrix comparing Module 13 (Conversation UI) and Module 14 (CRM Widget). It outlines which features are available in each module, highlighting differences in implementation due to UI constraints, technical limitations, or integration requirements. Key points include differences in conversation history display, data visualization methods, handling of plugin outputs, table formatting, animation effects, real-time update mechanisms, CRM integration capabilities, keyboard shortcut support, and offline functionality. The matrix also provides reasons for each difference, such as sidebar size constraints, CRM context awareness, and technical restrictions like content security policies.

nodes.title: 14.6 Module Access Map — What Module 14 Touches
nodes.summary:
This partial document section outlines the integration points between Module 14 (M14) and various backend modules within a platform. It details how M14 accesses each backend module, the communication method used (primarily REST APIs, often via the Platform API), and specific notes about each integration. Key points include:

- M14 maintains session state continuity with M13 via the M1 State Engine.
- Agent behavior is consistent across different UI surfaces due to indirect orchestration through M2.
- Data integration (M4) supports session resolution and permission validation.
- Multi-tenancy (M5) allows for tenant-specific branding in the widget.
- Plugin execution (M12) is handled via the Platform API, with outputs rendered inline.
- Feedback signals (M16) include both standard and CRM-specific events.
- Authentication and roles (M18) leverage OAuth and JWT, supporting seamless SSO between CRM and the platform.
- All REST API calls from M14 are routed through the M20 API Gateway, with separate rate limits from M13.

Overall, the section provides a mapping of how M14 interacts with core backend services, emphasizing session management, integration consistency, and secure, branded, and rate-limited API communication.

structure.title: Module 15: Admin Portal
structure.prefix_summary:
# Module 15: Admin Portal

Module 15 is the administrative interface used by Sales Ops teams and platform administrators to configure, manage, and monitor the Sales Intelligence Platform. Unlike Modules 13 and 14 (which serve sales reps during customer conversations), Module 15 is a traditional web application with forms, tables, editors, and dashboards. It communicates exclusively via REST API (Platform API) and has no real-time requirements.

| Who Uses Module 15? The Admin Portal serves two personas. Sales Ops / Admin: the primary user, responsible for configuring business rules, managing the knowledge base, setting up integrations, and monitoring adoption. They access all seven admin sections. Platform Super Admin: an internal role for cross-tenant support, used by the platform vendor’s customer success team. They can view tenant configurations, run diagnostics, and assist with onboarding. This role is enforced by M18 (Auth & Roles). |
| --- |

nodes.title: 15.1 Admin Sections Overview
nodes.summary: This partial document provides an overview of the main administrative sections within a platform, detailing their purposes, associated backend modules, and supported CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations. The sections covered include: Knowledge Base Management (handling documents and their relationships), Integration Setup (connecting and configuring CRM/ERP integrations), Business Rules (building and testing tenant-specific logic), Agent Configuration (managing workflow agents and their parameters), User Management (handling user accounts and roles), Discovery Framework (customizing discovery processes per tenant), and Usage Analytics (viewing admin-level metrics). Each section specifies its primary backend module and outlines the available administrative actions, highlighting which operations are supported for each area.

nodes.title: 15.2 KB Management — Deep Dive
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 15.2 KB Management — Deep Dive

The Knowledge Base Management section is the most complex admin surface. It is the interface through which tenant administrators populate M3 (KB Engine) with product information, competitive intelligence, pricing rules, and sales collateral that agents and plugins consume.

nodes.title: 15.2.1 Document Upload Pipeline
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes the "Document Upload Pipeline" for an admin interface. It outlines a step-by-step process for uploading documents (PDF, DOCX, XLSX, CSV, Markdown) to a platform. The main points covered include: 

1. Upload: Admins upload files, which are validated for type, size, and malware before being sent to the backend ingestion pipeline.
2. Processing: The backend processes documents by chunking, generating embeddings, extracting metadata (such as titles, product mentions, and categories), and updating vector and keyword indexes. The UI provides real-time status updates and error messages if needed.
3. Review: Admins can review and edit extracted metadata, assign product tags and categories, with auto-suggestions provided. Changes update the backend metadata and recalculate relationships if tags change.
4. Publish: Admins publish the document, making it available to agents and plugins via the API. The UI confirms publication and lists the document as published.

The document details both the admin actions and backend processing at each step, along with the corresponding UI feedback.

nodes.title: 15.2.2 Visual Relationship Editor
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the Visual Relationship Editor, a graph-based user interface that allows administrators to define and manage relationships between products within the M3 knowledge graph. These defined relationships influence the recommendations made by various AI agents, such as cross-sell, upsell, renewal, and solution-building agents. The document outlines different types of product relationships—complements, upgrades_to, replaces, bundles_with, and competes_with—explaining their meanings, the specific agents affected, and providing examples for each. The editor enables more intelligent and context-aware product recommendations by encoding how products interact, upgrade, or compete with each other.

nodes.title: 15.3 Integration Setup
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 15.3 Integration Setup

The Integration Setup section is where admins connect the platform to external systems (CRM, ERP) via Module 4 (Data Integration). The admin portal provides a guided wizard that walks through each step of the integration process.

nodes.title: 15.3.1 Connection Wizard Flow
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines the step-by-step flow of a Connection Wizard used by admins to integrate CRM/ERP platforms (such as Salesforce, HubSpot, SAP, Oracle) with another system. It details both the admin actions and backend processing for each step: selecting the platform, authenticating via OAuth, mapping fields, configuring sync settings, testing the connection, and activating the integration. The document also describes integration health monitoring features, including a dashboard displaying sync status, error counts, and latency, as well as automated alerts and remediation guidance for common integration issues.

nodes.title: 15.4 Business Rules — Visual Rule Builder
nodes.prefix_summary: This partial document describes the "Business Rules — Visual Rule Builder" feature, which allows administrators to define custom, tenant-specific logic for agent interactions without coding. It explains that rules are managed in the M5 business_rules layer and evaluated during conversations. The visual builder uses a drag-and-drop interface with different types of blocks: Condition Blocks (IF statements based on session or customer data), Action Blocks (THEN statements to modify agent behavior or trigger actions), and Exception Blocks (UNLESS clauses to override rules in specific cases). The document also covers rule Priority (determining execution order when multiple rules apply) and Scope (specifying which agents and workflows the rule affects or excludes). Examples are provided for each component.

nodes.title: 15.4.1 Test and Preview
nodes.summary:
### 15.4.1 Test and Preview

Before activating a rule, admins can test it against sample scenarios. The admin selects a test customer (from real CRM data, anonymized if needed) and a test agent workflow. The platform runs the rule evaluation and shows: which conditions matched, which actions would fire, which recommendations would be filtered/modified, and what the rep would see differently. This prevents admins from deploying rules that accidentally block all recommendations or create contradictory constraints.

nodes.title: 15.5 Agent Configuration
nodes.summary: This partial document section explains how administrators can configure platform-defined agents (M6–M11) within their tenant. It details the configurable aspects of agent behavior, including enabling/disabling agents, setting trigger thresholds, assigning priority weights, customizing quick action sets, and selecting discovery dimensions. Each configuration option is described with its purpose, an example, and the specific storage location in the tenant configuration. Admins cannot create or delete agents but have granular control over how agents operate for their tenant’s needs.

nodes.title: 15.6 User Management
nodes.prefix_summary: This partial document outlines the User Management section for a platform, focusing on how user roles are defined and what permissions they have. It clarifies that this system manages platform-specific access and does not replace the CRM’s user management. The document presents a table detailing different user roles (Sales Rep, Sales Manager, Sales Ops/Admin, Executive, Platform Super Admin), specifying for each: which platform modules they can access, their functional capabilities within those modules, and the scope of data they can view or manage. Permissions are enforced by dedicated modules (e.g., M18 for roles and data scoping, M5 for tenant isolation), and data access is restricted according to role and organizational hierarchy. The section emphasizes security, data isolation, and the separation of duties across user types.

nodes.title: 15.6.1 User Onboarding Flow
nodes.summary:
### 15.6.1 User Onboarding Flow

When an admin invites a new user: admin enters the user’s email and selects a role. The Platform API creates a pending user record in M18. An invitation email is sent with a one-time setup link. The user clicks the link and authenticates via the tenant’s SSO provider (configured in M18). On first login, M4 syncs the user’s CRM profile to determine account assignments. The user’s data scope is automatically set based on CRM assignments. The admin can override account assignments manually if needed.

nodes.title: 15.7 Discovery Framework Configuration
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes how administrators can configure the Discovery Framework that underpins the Discovery Progress component in Module 13. It outlines the customizable elements of the framework, including the ability to rename, add, or remove discovery dimensions (such as Business Challenges or Budget Authority), adjust the weighting of each dimension, set custom completion thresholds for each dimension, assign specific dimensions to different agent roles, and customize the discovery questions associated with each dimension. The configuration options allow organizations to tailor the discovery process to their industry and workflow needs, directly impacting how agents assess discovery progress and transition to recommendation phases.

nodes.title: 15.8 Usage Analytics (Admin View)
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the "Usage Analytics (Admin View)" section, which provides administrators with metrics focused on platform health, user adoption, data quality, agent effectiveness, plugin usage, and compliance. It distinguishes these metrics from executive dashboards by emphasizing operational insights rather than ROI. The document details specific metric categories, their data sources, and associated action triggers for admins, such as sending training reminders for low adoption, prompting document updates for stale knowledge bases, reviewing agent configurations for low effectiveness, managing plugins based on usage and error rates, and addressing compliance issues like PII detection.

nodes.title: 15.9 Module Access Map — What Module 15 Touches
nodes.summary: This partial document provides a table mapping out which backend modules are accessed by Module 15, specifying the corresponding admin sections, the types of operations performed, and the communication methods used. It details how Module 15 interacts with various backend components such as orchestrators, knowledge base engines, data integration, multi-tenancy, feedback and analytics engines, authentication, compliance, and the API gateway. The document highlights the scope of CRUD operations, configuration management, analytics access, and security/audit functions, all primarily facilitated via REST APIs, with some modules supporting multipart uploads or OAuth callbacks. The table clarifies the integration points and operational boundaries between Module 15 and other system modules.

structure.title: Shared Backend Services
structure.prefix_summary:
# Shared Backend Services

All three interface modules communicate with the backend through a shared service layer. Understanding these services clarifies how M13, M14, and M15 connect to the rest of the platform.

nodes.title: Shared.1 Platform API
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the Shared.1 Platform API, a unified REST API serving multiple interface modules. It explains that the API is implemented behind an API Gateway (Module 20), which manages rate limiting, authentication, request routing, and response caching. All HTTP requests from modules M13, M14, and M15 are routed through this gateway. The document provides a table summarizing the main API domains, their consumers, key endpoints, and authentication requirements. Covered domains include Sessions, Plugins, Feedback, Knowledge Base, Integrations, Tenant Config, Users, and Analytics, each with specific endpoints and JWT-based authentication scopes (rep, admin, or executive). The document highlights how different modules interact with the API and the security measures in place for each domain.

nodes.title: Shared.2 WebSocket Service
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the architecture and key concerns of the Shared.2 WebSocket Service, which provides real-time communication for Module 13 (Conversation UI) by maintaining persistent connections with active user sessions. It details how the service subscribes to state changes from the State Engine (M1) and routes updates to clients based on session IDs. The document covers several implementation aspects: scaling (using Redis-backed session affinity and automatic reconnection with state sync), authentication (JWT validation and token refresh handling), message ordering (sequence numbers and recovery from missed events), backpressure management (buffering and state snapshotting for slow clients), and multi-tab support (ensuring consistent state across multiple browser tabs for the same session).

nodes.title: Shared.3 Auth Service
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the Shared.3 Auth Service, which centralizes authentication and authorization for various interface modules by wrapping Module 18 (Auth & Roles). It outlines how each module (Conversation UI, CRM Widget, Admin Portal) uses a distinct authentication flow but ultimately issues a JWT validated by the Platform API. The document details the authentication process, token contents, and session duration for each module, highlighting differences such as SSO methods, session context, MFA enforcement, and security measures like session length and re-authentication requirements for sensitive actions.

structure.title: Cross-Module Interaction Summary
structure.summary:
This partial document presents a comprehensive summary of cross-module interactions within a backend system, focusing on how three interface modules—Conversation UI (M13), CRM Widget (M14), and Admin Portal (M15)—consume and interact with twenty backend modules (M1–M20). The main points covered include:

- A tabular mapping of each backend module’s integration points with the three interface modules, specifying whether access is direct, indirect, or absent.
- Details on the communication methods used (e.g., WebSocket, REST polling) and the nature of data exchanged (real-time sync, CRUD operations, analytics, etc.).
- Clarification of which modules provide core functionalities such as state management, orchestration, knowledge base access, data integration, multi-tenancy, agent/plugin execution, feedback collection, analytics, authentication, compliance, and API routing.
- Differentiation of access levels and capabilities for each interface module, highlighting which modules are primary consumers, which have read/write or read-only access, and which rely on indirect consumption via other modules.
- The document serves as a definitive reference for understanding backend capability exposure across different UI surfaces, supporting both technical integration and security/compliance considerations.

structure.title: Key Technical Decisions Summary
structure.summary: This partial document summarizes key technical decisions made for different modules (M13, M14, M15) in a system, focusing on transport protocols, state management, context detection, security, testing, and API gateway architecture. It outlines the chosen solutions (e.g., WebSocket for real-time updates, REST for admin operations, platform-specific SDKs for context detection), the rationale behind each choice (such as CRM platform restrictions, need for real-time updates, or security requirements), and alternatives that were considered and rejected (like REST polling, client-side state management, or synthetic test data). The document emphasizes reliability, security, operational simplicity, and alignment with CRM platform constraints.
